problem: RL-trained embodied agents optimize one fixed hand-designed reward, so adapting to diverse user preferences (quiet, urgent, thorough) requires re-training; prior preference-learning methods are limited to simple low-dimensional tasks.
motivation: Users have different, context-dependent priorities over navigation behavior (speed, exploration, safety) and non-experts cannot hand-craft rewards. Reducing personalization to inferring a low-dimensional reward-weight vector lets a single frozen policy serve many users.
key_idea: Train one weight-conditioned multi-objective RL policy over randomly sampled reward weights, then personalize at test time by inferring the weight vector from human demonstrations, trajectory-comparison feedback, or LLM-parsed language instructions, with no policy fine-tuning.
insight: A single policy trained on random simplex weights reproduces (and often beats) fixed-weight specialist policies while covering the whole preference space at far lower training cost; e.g. house-exploration weighting gives SR 0.680 vs 0.200 for the corresponding Prioritized EmbCLIP policy. Group trajectory comparison is far more feedback-efficient than pairwise: M=5 with 10 queries gives 0.862 cosine sim, similar to pairwise with 500 queries (0.897). The codebook weight encoder stabilizes training (57.8% lower success std vs raw), while the integer lookup table causes ambiguity in weight prediction.
method: Weight-conditioned MORL policy: single-policy MORL with scalarized reward w^T r, w sampled uniformly from the K-simplex each episode; multi-objective DD-PPO trained in AllenAct
Visual/goal encoder: frozen CLIP ResNet-50 (2048x7x7) fused with a 32-dim goal embedding, CNN to 1568-d, then GRU policy
Reward weight encoder: FFNN expands w to 30-d, passed through a codebook of 30 learnable K*12-dim codes, concatenated into the recurrent policy

Demonstration-based weight inference: maximize the action log-likelihood of a human demo under pi(a|s;w), gradient descent from multiple initializations including uniform, optimizing only K parameters

Preference feedback: Bradley-Terry likelihood over pairwise trajectory comparisons; novel group trajectory comparison compares groups of M trajectories generated from weight regions, each answer giving a hyperplane constraint for constrained optimization, with a probabilistic guarantee
Language instructions: ChatGPT with in-context examples (6 human-written) and chain-of-thought outputs spiked weight vectors from the task and objective definitions
Objectives: ObjectNav has 5 (time efficiency, path efficiency, house exploration, object exploration, safety); FleeNav has 3 (time, exploration, safety)

setting.backbone: CLIP ResNet-50 (frozen) + CNN + GRU policy trained with multi-objective DD-PPO; ChatGPT (frozen, few-shot) for language-to-weight
setting.training_data: RL in simulation: ProcTHOR ObjectNav 130M steps over 10k houses; ProcTHOR FleeNav 50M steps over 10k houses; RoboTHOR 100M steps over 60 houses; no extra data
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: MoveAhead, RotateRight, RotateLeft, Done, LookUp, LookDown
setting.privileged: none at policy test time (sub-rewards use simulator info only for training/evaluation); weight prediction uses human demos/feedback/instructions

numbers_note: Success/SPL are reported per reward-weight configuration, not as a single headline number. Weight-prediction results (cosine similarity, GGI, win rate) are in Tables 3/4/7 and are not benchmark navigation metrics.
results: One promptable policy matches or beats per-objective Prioritized EmbCLIP, e.g. house-exploration prioritization gives SR 0.680 vs 0.200 and path-efficiency prioritization gives the best SPL (0.543), at much lower training cost. Group comparison (M=2, 25 queries) reaches 0.935 cosine similarity and the highest human win rate (0.650), ChatGPT with CoT gives 0.614 similarity, and demos give 0.707 from a single demonstration.
limitations: Assumes static, linear preferences over a small fixed set of hand-designed objectives
Evaluated only in simulation on small validation sets (100 episodes); no real-robot experiments
Weight prediction from demos is ambiguous and LLM predictions are the weakest (about 0.5–0.6 cosine similarity)
builds_on: Deep RL from human preferences (Christiano et al.)
